new_statements.quote: The stress rules throughout the Uradhi dialects appear to be fairly uniform. The most important generalisations regarding stress are: (i) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable, (i.e. third syllable from the end), of a word that contains only short vowels. Words of three syllables or less are therefore stressed on the initial syllable. Examples (from the Atampaya dialect): /áma/ 'person' ... /ukúmala/ 'sweet potato' /ayparúmpiwa/ 'sparrowhawk' (ii) In the case of words containing long vowels, it is always the long vowels that receive primary stress, regardless of their position in the word. (Note that it is possible to have a word that contains two primary stresses.) ... /ití:na/ 'thigh' /amá:ka/ 'message stick' /tá:rá:namu/ 'reef-GEN'
new_statements.citation: Crowley, Terry. 1983. Uradhi. In R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds.), Handbook of Australian Languages, vol. 3, 306-428. Canberra: ANU Press / Amsterdam: John Benjamins.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In all three Uradhi dialects (Atampaya, Angkamuthi, Yadhaykenu): if a word has only short vowels, primary stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable (hence the initial syllable in words of one to three syllables); if a word contains long vowels, every long vowel carries primary stress wherever it stands, so a word may have two primary stresses.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; Crowley gives no statement on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the rules are hedged as 'appear to be fairly uniform' across dialects and 'the most important generalisations'. All illustrative words are Atampaya. Relevant for Angkamuthi: long vowels there are 'much less restricted' and occur even in final syllables of underived words (p.318-319, /uyuwa:/ 'hard beefwood'), which under rule (ii) would be final-stressed; lengthening suffixes (reciprocal /-:(t)pa/, reflexive /-:nti/, comitative -:yma, excessive /-:ta/) create stressed long vowels late in the word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain ('of a word', 'position in the word'); examples are citation forms. Note the pervasive word-final sandhi (2.4) alters surface syllable count at utterance end, which Crowley does not relate to stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley 1983 describes three 'Uradhi dialects' jointly: Atampaya (atam1239), Angkamuthi (angg1238) and Yadhaykenu (yadh1237); Glottolog 5.1 treats each as a separate language under Uradhic. The stress statement is made for 'throughout the Uradhi dialects' but every example is from Atampaya; no Angkamuthi-specific stress example is given. Angkamuthi differs in allowing distinctive long vowels in final syllables (p.318-319, e.g. /uyuwa:/ 'hard beefwood'), which by rule (ii) would carry primary stress word-finally. The catalog already holds the same passage under atam1239; this record extends it to angg1238 on the strength of Crowley's explicit 'throughout the Uradhi dialects'. Hale 1976 concerns the Uradhi-proper dialect (urad1239, Glottolog bookkeeping), not Angkamuthi.

sources.note: Section 2.3 Stress, p.322: stress rules uniform throughout the Uradhi dialects (Atampaya, Angkamuthi, Yadhaykenu); primary stress antepenultimate in words with only short vowels (initial if three syllables or fewer); long vowels always take primary stress regardless of position, two primary stresses possible. Examples from Atampaya only. p.318-319: Angkamuthi permits distinctive long vowels even in final syllables.
